title: Why the App Router caches what it caches
excerpt: Most caching surprises in the App Router come from one question the framework asks about every route: can this be rendered before a request arrives?

children.text: Most caching surprises in the App Router trace back to a single question the framework asks about every route: can this page be rendered before a request arrives? If it can, it is rendered once and reused. If it cannot, it is rendered per request.
Static until proven dynamic

A route starts out eligible for static rendering. It stays that way until the code reads something that only exists at request time: cookies, request headers, or the search parameters of the URL. The moment a component reads one of those, the route has to wait for a request.
That is why a page can flip from fast to slow after an innocent change. Nobody asked for dynamic rendering; a helper deep in the tree read a cookie.
Data has its own clock

Rendering and data are cached separately. A static page can still hold data that expires, and a dynamic page can still reuse cached data. Time-based revalidation says how old data may get. Tag-based revalidation lets a write mark exactly the data it affected as stale.
Use a time window when the source changes on its own schedule.
Use tags when your own code performs the write and knows what it touched.
Debug by asking the same question
When a page is slower or staler than expected, ask what it reads at request time and what its data is tagged with. The answer is almost always one of those two lists.

title: Chunk size is a retrieval decision, not a storage one
excerpt: Pick chunk sizes from the questions you expect, not from what fits the database. The unit you retrieve is the unit the model gets to reason over.

children.text: Chunking is usually decided early and by convenience: a round number of tokens that fits comfortably in the vector store. But the chunk is the unit you retrieve, and the unit you retrieve is the unit the model reasons over.
Too small loses the answer
A short chunk matches a query sharply, but it often holds the sentence that names the concept and not the sentence that explains it. The model then answers from a fragment.
Too large drowns the answer

A long chunk contains the explanation, but its embedding averages over everything else in it. It ranks lower for specific questions, and when it is retrieved it spends the context window on text that does not help.
Size from the questions
Write down twenty real questions and the passage that answers each one. Measure those passages. That distribution, not the database, tells you where to start.
Split on the structure the source already has: headings, paragraphs, timestamps.
Keep a little overlap so an answer that straddles a boundary survives.
Re-run the same twenty questions after every change.

title: Read the query plan before you add an index
excerpt: An index is a guess about how the planner will run a query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE turns the guess into a measurement, and it takes seconds.

children.text: When a query is slow, adding an index feels like the obvious fix. Sometimes it is. Often the planner was never going to use it, and the table now pays for it on every write.
Ask the planner first
EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL intends to use. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows what actually happened, including real row counts and timings for every step.
Look for the gap between estimate and reality

The most useful number on the plan is the difference between estimated rows and actual rows. When they differ by orders of magnitude, the planner chose its strategy for a different query than the one you ran. Fresh statistics often fix that without any new index.
Then index the step that hurts
A sequential scan that discards most rows is the classic index candidate.
A sort on a large result may want an index in the sort order.
A nested loop over many rows may want an index on the join key.
Change one thing, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE again, and keep the index only if the plan and the timing both improved.

title: Why Vortex exists
excerpt: YouTube already holds world-class teaching. What it lacks is the structure that turns watching into learning: order, checkpoints and a way to know you got it.

children.text: Some of the best teaching in the world is free, and most of it is on YouTube. A patient engineer explaining context windows, a chef showing how dough should feel, a professor working a proof on a whiteboard. The teaching is there. What is missing is everything a course wraps around it.
The problem is not content
A learner who opens YouTube to study faces three problems that have nothing to do with the quality of any single video.
No order. Search and recommendations rank videos for engagement, not for what you need to know first. You jump from an advanced talk to a beginner recap and back.
No checkpoints. Nothing marks where you stopped or what you have already covered, so revisiting a topic means starting from scratch.
No evidence. Watching feels like learning. Without a question at the end, there is no way to tell whether it was.

The third problem matters most. Decades of research show that the feeling of fluency while watching is a poor guide to what you will remember, and that answering questions is one of the most effective ways to learn. We cover that research in the Learning Science notes.

body.name: vortex-before-after
body.caption: The same videos, before and after: scattered on YouTube, then ordered into modules with saved progress and a quiz per lesson.

children.text: What Vortex adds
Vortex does not make videos. It gives existing ones the structure of a course.
Order. Courses are authored in modules, and every lesson points at one video. Module and lesson numbers come from that order, so "Lesson 2.3" always means the same thing.
Search that lands on the second. Ask in plain English and Vortex ranks the lessons that teach it, opening the video at the moment the topic starts.
Progress that remembers. Your place in each video is saved to the second, and completed lessons are marked.
A quiz after every video. Answers are graded on the server, you see which answers you missed, and you can retake it.
Plans for everything else. Describe a goal that is not in the catalog, and Vortex designs a syllabus and matches each lesson to a real YouTube video.

body.text: Every video still plays in YouTube's own player, and every lesson names the channel that made it. Vortex organizes teaching; it does not take it.

children.text: What we optimize for
Most video platforms optimize for watch time. That is the wrong target for learning: the goal of a lesson is to be finished, understood and remembered, and ideally to take less time rather than more.

So Vortex measures different moments. The analytics events we record are the ones that indicate learning: a lesson viewed and completed, how far a video is watched, a search performed and the result it led to. There is no autoplaying feed of recommendations. When you finish a module, the product should get out of your way.
Principles we hold ourselves to
Grounded. Search never invents a lesson, a title or a timestamp; every card is read back from the dataset.
Credited. The creator is named on every lesson, and playback stays with YouTube.
Private by default. Your progress and plans belong to your account and are only written through authenticated server routes.
Honest. If the data does not support a claim, the interface does not make it: no fake learner counts, no invented reviews.
The rest of the Inside Vortex series explains how those principles show up in the architecture, the security model and the way we handle creators' work.

title: How Vortex is built
excerpt: Two workspaces, one private dataset, and a search pipeline where the language model proposes and the database decides.

children.text: Vortex is a Next.js application in front of a private Sanity dataset, with authentication by Clerk and analytics by PostHog. This note walks through how the pieces fit, and why each boundary sits where it does.
Two workspaces

The repository holds two standalone projects. The Studio is a Sanity Studio: schema and content authoring, nothing else. The web workspace is the Next.js site: pages, the search route, and every server-side integration. Keeping them apart means the Studio can be deployed and upgraded on its own, and TypeGen can generate types for the web app straight from the schema and the GROQ queries.

body.name: system-architecture
body.caption: The browser only talks to the Next.js server. Every credential lives on the server, which talks to Sanity, Clerk, the language model, the YouTube Data API and PostHog.

children.text: Content is read-only, state is not

Courses, lessons, categories and video documents are content. Pages render them through one server-only fetch helper that reads the private dataset with a token and caches by tag. None of that is writable from the site.

Learner state is different: progress, enrollments, quiz attempts, plans, ideas and votes. It is keyed to the Clerk user id and written only by server routes that hold a separate write token. The browser never writes anything directly.
Search: the model proposes, the dataset decides
Search is the heart of Vortex, and the place where a language model could most easily go wrong. The route runs two passes at once.

A model pass. The model connects to the Sanity Context MCP server, which exposes the schema and a GROQ query tool scoped by a filter to content types only. It writes queries, reads what comes back, and returns structured hits: a lesson id, a rank, a reason and, for a video moment, the second it starts.
A keyword and chapter pass. A deterministic query matches the words of the question against lesson titles, key points and notes, and against the chapter labels and transcript chunks of each video.

body.name: search-pipeline
body.caption: Both passes run in parallel and are merged to one hit per lesson. Grounding then rebuilds every card from the dataset.

children.text: The model pass is time-boxed. If it is slow or over its token budget, the keyword results ship on their own rather than the learner waiting on a spinner.
Grounding

The model contributes ids and seconds, never display text. Before anything reaches the browser, grounding re-reads each lesson from Sanity by id: the title, the course, the module and lesson label, the duration and the thumbnail. A hit whose id does not resolve is dropped. A "video" hit without a real start second is downgraded to a lesson hit, because a moment with no timestamp has nothing to link to. Sorting by relevance, duration or recency happens afterwards, in code, so re-sorting never costs another model call.

body.text: A hallucinated title cannot reach the page, because the page never shows anything the model wrote except its short reason for the match.

children.text: Video intelligence, built offline

Timestamps come from video documents built by offline tooling, one per unique video. Each holds the video's chapters as a table of contents and its captions split into short timestamped chunks. Search matches chapters first, because chapter labels are clean, and falls back to transcript chunks only when no chapter matches.

body.name: ingestion-pipeline
body.caption: Ingestion never runs in the request path. At query time, search fetches only the few chunks that match, never a whole transcript.

children.text: Personal plans

Plans are the one feature that reaches outside the catalog at request time. When a signed-in learner describes a goal, the server asks the model for a syllabus, then looks up a video for each lesson through the official YouTube Data API with safe search set to strict and only embeddable videos allowed. Each learner can create a limited number of plans per day, counted from the dataset. A lesson's quiz is generated from that video's captions the first time it is opened, and cached on the plan.
Why these boundaries
The browser holds no secret, so there is nothing to leak from it.
Every write has one door, a server route, so it can be authenticated, validated and rate limited in one place.
The language model has read-only, scoped access and no path to the page except through grounding.
The next note looks at those doors in detail.

title: Security at Vortex: tokens, trust boundaries and the write path
excerpt: Where every secret lives, which way requests are allowed to flow, and the ordered checks each write passes before it touches the dataset.

children.text: A learning platform holds less sensitive data than a bank, but it still holds people's accounts, their progress and anything they write. This note describes how Vortex protects them, concretely enough that you could check the code against it.
Secrets stay on the server

Vortex uses a handful of credentials: a Sanity read token, a Sanity write token, the Clerk secret key, keys for the language model provider, and a YouTube Data API key. All of them are read only in server modules. The modules that use them import "server-only", which makes the build fail if client code ever imports them, so a leak is a compile error rather than a production incident.
Only two keys ever reach the browser, and both are public by design: Clerk's publishable key and PostHog's project key.

body.name: trust-boundaries
body.caption: The browser holds only public keys. Every secret stays on the server, and the private dataset is reachable only from there.

children.text: A private dataset

The Sanity dataset is private. Nothing, not even published course content, can be read without a token. Pages fetch on the server, so a visitor receives rendered HTML and the fields a page chose to show, never raw documents.
Authentication

Sign-in is Clerk. Browsing, search and every lesson page are public. Private surfaces, meaning My Learning, plans and every write route, are gated by Clerk's middleware, and each route handler checks the session again itself. A route never takes a user id from the request body; the learner is always whoever the session says is signed in.
The write path

Every write goes through a server route, and every route applies its checks in order, rejecting as early as it can. The Ideas board, where learners post and vote on feature ideas, shows the full sequence.

body.name: write-path-guards
body.caption: Each gate rejects with its own status code before any work is done.

children.text: Same origin and JSON only. A request whose Origin header does not match the site is refused (403), and anything that is not application/json is refused (415). A plain HTML form on another site cannot produce either.
A session. No Clerk session, no write (401).
A strict schema. Zod validates the body and rejects unknown fields, so a client cannot smuggle in a status, an owner or a moderation flag (400). Bodies are size-capped before parsing.
A rate limit. Limits are counted from the dataset rather than from memory, so they hold across serverless instances: three ideas a day per learner, five plans a day (429).
Server-set fields. The server assigns ids, timestamps, ownership and status. A new idea arrives as pending and is invisible to others until someone on the team approves it.
The write itself, with the server token.
Concurrency: compare-and-set

Progress is written often and sometimes in parallel, for example when two tabs save a video position at once. Progress writes use compare-and-set: read the document, compute the change, and commit only if the revision is still the one that was read. On a conflict the route re-reads and retries with a short randomized pause. Two saves never silently overwrite each other with stale state.
Grades are computed, never accepted
When you submit a quiz, the browser sends your answers, not your score. The server grades them against the stored quiz. A stored grade can never be one your answers did not earn.
Untrusted text

Anything a learner writes, such as an idea's title and description, is stored and rendered as plain text. It is never parsed as HTML or markdown and never injected into the page, and invisible control characters are stripped on the way in. Rich text written by the team in the Studio is rendered through Portable Text components that only allow http and https links.
Headers and embeds

Every response carries a baseline of security headers: nosniff, a strict-origin referrer policy, a same-origin frame policy, and a permissions policy that turns off the camera, microphone and geolocation. Video embeds are built from a parsed video id, never from a stored URL, and YouTube videos load from the privacy-enhanced youtube-nocookie.com domain.

body.text: There is no Content Security Policy yet. Clerk, PostHog and the video embeds each need their own allowances, and a wrong policy breaks sign-in or playback silently, so it will be added deliberately and tested rather than guessed.

children.text: The search model is read-only

The language model behind search holds no write token and has no mutation tool. The Context server it talks to is scoped by a filter to content types, so learner state such as progress, plans and ideas is outside what it can see.

title: Creators, copyright and how Vortex uses YouTube
excerpt: Vortex organizes other people's teaching, so how it treats that work matters. What we do, what we never do, and where the line sits.

children.text: Every lesson on Vortex is a video someone else made. That makes one question more important than any feature: how do we build on creators' work while respecting it? This note describes our practice plainly.

body.text: This describes how Vortex is designed. It is not legal advice, and copyright rules differ between countries.

children.text: Playback stays on YouTube

Vortex never downloads, re-hosts or re-encodes a video. Lessons play in YouTube's own embedded player, the same player YouTube offers anyone who wants to share a video on their site. The video file, the player and its controls stay YouTube's. When a search result links to a moment, Vortex passes the start second to that player through YouTube's own start parameter; it does not cut or clip the video.

Embedding follows the creator's own choice. A creator who turns off embedding for a video stops it playing on external sites, including this one, and the plan builder only ever asks the YouTube Data API for embeddable videos.

body.name: creator-flow
body.caption: The creator's video reaches the learner through YouTube's player, with the channel credited. Captions feed an internal search index. Downloading or re-hosting is not part of the design.

children.text: Credit on every lesson

Each video document records the channel that published it. Every lesson shows "by" that channel, and every course lists the creators behind its videos, most-used first. When a course is built mostly from one channel's work, that channel is the first thing you see after the title.
How transcripts are used

Search needs to know what is said, and when. Offline tooling reads a video's captions and splits them into short, timestamped chunks stored on an internal video document. That index is used to find the second a topic starts.
Transcripts are never shown to learners whole. At most, a result shows a chapter label or a one-line reason for the match.
The search model is only ever given a few matching chunks per video, never a full transcript.
For personal plans, a quiz is generated from a video's captions the first time the lesson is opened, and cached privately on that learner's plan.
Adding, not replacing

The value Vortex adds is order, progress, quizzes and search: things that make a creator's explanation easier to find and more likely to be finished and remembered. The explanation itself remains the creator's, delivered by YouTube, with their name on it. If Vortex ever stopped being able to say that honestly about a feature, the feature would be wrong.
What creators can expect
Their video plays in YouTube's player, never a copy.
Their channel is named on every lesson that uses it.
Their embedding settings are respected.
Their words are indexed for search, not republished.

title: Spacing: why cramming works tonight and fails next month
excerpt: The same study time, spread out, beats one long session. The best gap depends on how long you need to remember, and research tells us roughly how to pick it.

children.text: In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and tracked how quickly he forgot them. Two findings from that work have held up for well over a century: forgetting is fast at first and then slows, and reviewing material brings it back and slows the next round of forgetting.

body.name: forgetting-reviews
body.caption: Illustrative shape, not data: one session decays quickly; spaced reviews restore recall and flatten the curve after each one.

children.text: The spacing effect

The spacing effect is the finding that the same amount of study produces better long-term retention when it is spread across sessions than when it is massed into one. It is among the most replicated results in cognitive psychology. A large review by Cepeda and colleagues (2006) pooled hundreds of comparisons from verbal recall studies and found the advantage consistently.

Cramming is not useless. Massed study can produce good performance on a test given soon afterwards. It fails when the goal is to still know the material weeks or months later, which is the goal of almost all real learning.
How far apart?

The more practical question is how long to wait between sessions. Cepeda and colleagues (2008) ran a large study with 1,350 participants who learned facts, restudied them after a gap of up to 105 days, and were tested after a retention interval of up to 350 days.

body.name: spacing-ridgeline
body.caption: Cepeda et al. (2008): the best gap grows with how long you need to remember, but shrinks as a share of it.

children.text: The best gap depended on when the test came. To remember for about a week, the best gap was roughly 20 to 40 percent of that week, about one to three days. To remember for a year, it was roughly 5 to 10 percent; for a 350-day test, the best gap was 23 days. Gaps that were too short hurt more than gaps that were somewhat too long.

body.text: Decide how long you need to remember something, then review it after a gap of very roughly a tenth to a fifth of that time, and err toward longer rather than shorter.

children.text: Why spacing works

The leading explanations share an idea: a review is most useful when some forgetting has happened, because pulling a half-forgotten memory back takes effort, and that effort strengthens it. A review right after studying is easy and adds little. This is one of what Robert Bjork called desirable difficulties: conditions that make learning feel harder in the moment but improve retention.
How Vortex applies it
Courses are split into short lessons across modules, so a course is naturally studied over several sessions rather than one.
Progress saves your place to the second, so stopping and coming back later costs nothing.
Quizzes can be retaken, which turns a return visit into retrieval practice instead of rewatching. The next note covers why that matters.

title: Testing is a learning event, not just a measurement
excerpt: Pulling an answer out of memory changes the memory. Students who were tested remembered more a week later than students who reread, even though rereading won in the short run.

children.text: We usually think of a test as a thermometer: it measures learning that happened somewhere else. A large body of research says tests also cause learning. Retrieving an answer from memory strengthens that memory more than seeing the answer again. This is called the testing effect, or retrieval practice.
The classic experiment

Roediger and Karpicke (2006) had students learn short prose passages under three schedules in one session: read the passage four times; read it three times and then write down everything they could recall; or read it once and recall it three times. Students then took a final recall test either five minutes or one week later.

body.name: testing-effect
body.caption: Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Experiment 2. Rereading won after five minutes; recall practice won after a week.

children.text: After five minutes, more reading meant better recall: 83 percent for four readings against 71 percent for one reading and three recalls. After a week the order reversed: 40 percent for four readings, 56 percent for three readings and one recall, and 61 percent for one reading and three recalls. The students who had spent most of their time retrieving remembered half as much again as those who had spent it rereading.
The students also predicted the opposite. Those who reread repeatedly expected to remember more. Rereading makes material feel familiar, and familiarity is easy to mistake for knowledge.
Not just for facts

A common objection is that testing only helps rote memorization. Karpicke and Blunt (2011) compared retrieval practice with building concept maps, a technique designed to promote deep, connected understanding. On a test a week later, including questions that required inference, retrieval practice produced more learning than concept mapping. It did so even when the final test asked students to draw a concept map.

Meta-analyses agree. Adesope, Trevisan and Sundararajan (2017) pooled a large body of experiments and found practice testing outperformed restudying and other comparison activities across test formats, ages and settings. Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), reviewing ten common study techniques, rated practice testing one of only two with high utility; rereading and highlighting were rated low.

body.text: After you watch or read something, close it and try to recall or answer questions about it. The effort of retrieving is the point.

children.text: Making it work
Test before you feel ready. Retrieval that takes effort helps more than retrieval that is effortless.
Get feedback. Checking answers corrects errors and strengthens correct answers you were unsure of.
Space it out. Retrieval practice and spacing combine: quiz yourself again after a gap.
How Vortex applies it

Every Vortex lesson ends in a short quiz rather than a "next video" button. Answers are graded as soon as you submit, you see which answers you missed, and you can retake it until you pass, with your best grade kept. The quiz is not there to gatekeep; it is there because answering it is one of the most effective things you can do with the ten minutes after a video.

title: Why lessons are short and end in a question
excerpt: Across millions of viewing sessions, learners watched short videos to the end and abandoned long ones. Putting a question between segments roughly halved mind wandering.

children.text: Online video makes it easy to publish a ninety-minute lecture. Two lines of research suggest that is rarely the best way to teach with it: attention fades across long videos, and short questions between segments bring it back.
Attention by the numbers

Guo, Kim and Rubin (2014) analysed 6.9 million video-watching sessions across four edX courses. The clearest finding concerned length. Learners typically watched videos under about six minutes to the end. As videos got longer, the share watched fell: roughly half of a 9 to 12 minute video, and roughly a fifth of a 12 to 40 minute one. Across lengths, the median time learners spent watching was at most about six minutes.

body.name: engagement-by-length
body.caption: Guo, Kim & Rubin (2014): approximate median share of a video watched, by video length.

children.text: The authors recommended planning lessons in segments under six minutes, and they found that informal, personal videos held attention better than polished studio recordings of long lectures.

body.text: Engagement is not learning. A watched video is not necessarily understood. But a video that is abandoned halfway certainly teaches less than one that is finished.

children.text: Questions between segments

Szpunar, Khan and Schacter (2013) asked what happens when a recorded lecture is interrupted with short tests. Participants watched a 21-minute statistics lecture split into four segments. Some answered a few questions after every segment; others did not. At random moments, all were asked whether their mind was on the lecture.

body.name: interpolated-quizzes
body.caption: The same lecture, straight through or segmented with a short quiz after each part.

children.text: The tested group reported mind wandering about half as often, took notes about three times as often, and did better on the final test. They also reported less anxiety about that test. Knowing that a question is coming appears to keep people engaged with what they are watching.
Segmenting helps understanding too

Richard Mayer's research on multimedia learning describes a segmenting principle: people learn better when a complex explanation is presented in learner-paced segments rather than as one continuous stream. Mayer and Chandler (2001) found that letting learners control the pace of a narrated animation, piece by piece, improved their ability to apply what they learned to new problems.
How Vortex applies it
Lessons are single videos inside modules, so a course is a sequence of short, finishable steps rather than one long stream.
Every lesson ends in a short quiz, which acts as the question between segments.
Search opens a video at the exact second a topic starts, so you watch the few minutes you need rather than scrubbing through the rest.

title: The feeling of learning is a bad guide
excerpt: Students in active classes learned more but felt they learned less. Why fluency misleads us, and how to study against the grain of your own intuition.

children.text: If you want to know whether a study method works, the obvious move is to ask how well you feel you learned. The research is clear that this answer is often wrong, and wrong in a consistent direction.
Active classes, lower confidence

Deslauriers and colleagues (2019) taught introductory physics students in two ways: polished lectures by highly rated instructors, and active sessions where students worked through problems with guidance. Students then took the same test and reported how much they felt they had learned.

body.name: feeling-vs-learning
body.caption: Deslauriers et al. (2019): active classes against polished lectures, in standard deviations.

children.text: Students in the active classes scored about 0.46 standard deviations higher on the test, yet rated their feeling of learning about 0.56 standard deviations lower. The authors traced the gap to cognitive effort: active learning feels harder, and people read that difficulty as a sign of learning poorly.
Fluency is not knowledge

Watching a clear explanation feels fluent: every step makes sense as it happens. That fluency is real, but it is fluency of following, not of producing. The test of learning is whether you can produce the idea later without the explanation in front of you.

Kornell and Bjork (2008) found the same pattern with a different skill. People learned to recognize painters' styles either by seeing each artist's paintings together or mixed with other artists. Mixing produced better recognition of new paintings, but most participants believed the grouped version had worked better. We cover mixing in the note on interleaving.
Desirable difficulties

Bjork, Dunlosky and Kornell (2013) review why learners so often choose the less effective option. Rereading, highlighting and watching again all feel productive and produce quick familiarity. Spacing, testing and mixing feel slower and produce more errors in the moment, but lead to more durable learning. The difficulty is not a flaw in these methods; it is part of how they work.

body.text: If a study session felt effortless, be suspicious. If it felt effortful and you made mistakes, that is often a sign it is working.

children.text: A practical check
Close the video or the notes.
Explain the idea out loud, or answer a question about it, without looking.
Only then check. What you could not produce is what you have not yet learned.
How Vortex applies it

Vortex does not ask you how well you think you did. It asks you questions. The quiz after each lesson replaces the feeling of learning with evidence of it, and the grade tells you which parts to revisit.

title: Interleaving: mix your practice, even though it feels worse
excerpt: Doing all the problems of one kind before the next feels efficient. Mixing kinds made practice harder and tripled scores on a test a week later.

children.text: Textbooks and courses usually teach one kind of problem, then give a block of practice on exactly that kind, then move on. It feels efficient: by the tenth problem you are fast and accurate. Interleaving, mixing different kinds of problems together, feels worse. It is often much better.
The experiment

Rohrer and Taylor (2007) taught students how to find the volume of several kinds of geometric solids. Some practised in blocks, every problem of one kind before the next. Others practised the same problems shuffled together. During practice, the blocked group did better. On a test one week later the result flipped: the mixed group scored 63 percent, the blocked group 20 percent.

body.name: blocked-vs-interleaved
body.caption: Blocked and interleaved schedules use the same problems in a different order. Scores from Rohrer & Taylor (2007), one week later.

children.text: Why mixing helps

In a block, you always know which method to use: the same one as the last problem. The hard part of a real problem, recognizing what kind of problem it is, has been done for you. Mixed practice forces you to make that choice every time, and that choice is exactly what a later test, or a real task, will demand.

Interleaving also helps with learning categories. In Kornell and Bjork's (2008) study of painters' styles, seeing different artists mixed together helped people notice what distinguished them, and they were better at identifying the artist of paintings they had never seen.

body.text: Interleaving works best for material that is related but easily confused, such as similar problem types. Early on, a short block to learn a new method can help before you start mixing.

children.text: Using it
Once you have learned two or three related methods, practise them mixed rather than one at a time.
When reviewing, jump between modules instead of rewatching one in order.
Expect practice to feel slower and to make more mistakes. That is the mechanism, not a failure.
How Vortex applies it

Courses are ordered so each method is introduced once, in its place. For review, search lets you pull lessons from across modules and courses in one list, and quizzes can be retaken in any order, so mixing is always one search away.

title: Get it wrong first: pretesting and feedback
excerpt: Trying to answer before you have been taught improves what you learn next, even when your guesses are wrong, provided the right answer follows.

children.text: Being asked a question you cannot answer yet sounds like a waste of time. Research on pretesting suggests the opposite: an unsuccessful attempt to answer can make the answer, when it arrives, stick better.
The pretesting effect

Richland, Kornell and Kao (2009) had students read an essay about vision. Some first tried to answer questions about concepts in the essay before reading it; others simply spent that time reading. Across five experiments, the students who were pretested did better on a later test, even on the very questions they had got wrong on the pretest.
A likely explanation is that a question prepares the mind for its answer. Having searched for it, you notice it when it appears, and you connect it to what you already tried.

body.name: pretest-loop
body.caption: Try first, get feedback, study with the question in mind, then retrieve again later.

children.text: Feedback makes errors useful

Guessing only helps if the right answer follows. Hattie and Timperley (2007), synthesizing research on feedback in education, found it is among the most powerful influences on learning, and that the most useful feedback tells the learner where they are, where they are going, and what to do next, rather than only praising or grading.

Feedback also helps when you were right. Butler, Karpicke and Roediger (2008) found that feedback strengthened correct answers that learners had given with low confidence. Without it, a lucky guess stays a guess.

body.text: Before a lesson, ask yourself what you think the answer is. Afterwards, check it. A wrong guess plus a correction beats no guess at all.

children.text: Using it
Before you watch, read the lesson's key points and try to explain each one.
When you get a quiz question wrong, find the part of the video that covers it, then retake the quiz later rather than immediately.
Pay attention to answers you got right but were unsure of; they need feedback too.
How Vortex applies it

Each lesson lists what it will teach you, which invites a guess before you watch. The quiz marks which answers were wrong after you submit, and you can retake it until you pass. Personal plans get the same treatment: a quiz generated from each video, with the same grading and retakes.
